summary: 宪宗第三子；元和十五年宪宗崩（或云为宦官所弑），恒即位，改元长庆；长庆元年河北三镇复叛，元和之功尽失；长庆二年销兵之议，藩镇乘机坐大；游宴怠政，长庆四年崩。
summary_en: Third son of Xianzong; on Xianzong's death in the 15th year of Yuanhe — by the eunuchs' hand, some say — Heng took the throne, changing the era to Changqing; in the 1st year of Changqing the three garrisons of Hebei rose again, and the gains of Yuanhe were lost; in the 2nd year the debate over disbanding the armies let the feudatories grow. He played and feasted, neglecting government, and died in the 4th year of Changqing.

bio_md:
# 唐穆宗 · 主要事迹

李恒，宪宗第三子。元和十五年，宪宗暴崩（史多以为宦官陈弘志所弑），宦官拥立恒即位，改元长庆。穆宗即位之初，即「销兵」之议：以「天下已平」为由，罢诸镇兵额，崔植、杜元颖等议销兵——「销兵」之策，使藩镇之骄兵悍卒无所归，反成祸源。

长庆元年，卢龙、成德、魏博三镇相继复叛，朝廷讨伐无功——元和年间宪宗所收复之藩镇，一朝尽失；长庆二年，河北遂成「河朔故事」，割据之局自此不可复挽。穆宗「游宴怠政」，好击球、宴乐，「不亲政事」，政事委于宦官、权臣。

长庆四年，穆宗因服饵之疾崩，年三十。史评穆宗：「销兵误国，河北再乱。」元和之削藩，为唐室中兴之顶点；穆宗之销兵，为唐室中衰之转折——「销兵」二字，遂为史家之戒。穆宗以宴乐之君，承中兴之业而自毁之，唐室之衰，自穆宗而不可止。

> 参考：点校本《旧唐书》卷016《穆宗纪》。

bio_parts_en.value:
Li Heng, third son of Xianzong. In the 15th year of Yuanhe Xianzong died suddenly — the histories suspect the eunuch Chen Hongzhi — and the eunuchs set up Heng, changing the era to Changqing. His opening act was the "disbanding the armies": deeming the realm at peace, he cut the garrisons' strengths, Cui Zhi and Du Yuanying debating the reduction — and the disbanded troops, with nowhere to go, became the very seed of disaster.

In the 1st year of Changqing the three garrisons of Lulong, Chengde, and Weibo rose again, and the court's campaigns failed — the feudatories recovered under Xianzong's Yuanhe reign were lost at a stroke; in the 2nd year Hebei settled into its "old story," and the division could not be mended. Muzong "played and feasted, neglecting government," loving polo and banquets, leaving affairs to the eunuchs and the ministers.

He died in the 4th year of Changqing of an elixir-sickness, aged thirty. The histories say: "disbanding the armies misled the realm, and Hebei rose again." The Yuanhe cutting of the feudatories was the summit of the restoration; Muzong's disbanding was the turn of the decline — "disbanding the armies" became the historians' warning. A pleasure-loving sovereign who threw away a restored realm: the decline of Tang could no longer be stopped from his reign.

> References: the punctuated critical edition of the *Jiu Tangshu*, ch. 16 ("Benji of Emperor Muzong").
